The PM–engineering relationship

What each side owes the other, what the exchange is actually for, and the four ways it reliably breaks.

1 A Tuesday in Pune

On the morning of 11 February, Meera Raghunathan sat in a glass-walled room on the fourth floor of Vachan Insurance Cloud's office in Kharadi, Pune, with a printed email in front of her and no good answer to it. Vachan sells policy-administration and claims software to general insurers — the unglamorous plumbing that turns a motor accident into a settled claim. Meera, thirty-four, had owned the claims module for three years. The email was from the chief operating officer of a mid-sized insurer that had signed a ₹4.2 crore annual contract eleven weeks earlier. The insurer wanted digital motor-claims intake live before the start of the next financial year: six weeks away.

Across the table sat Arjun Sekhri, the engineering manager for the nine-person claims squad. He had spent the previous afternoon with two senior engineers pulling the estimate apart, and the number he brought was fourteen weeks. Not fourteen weeks of stubbornness — fourteen weeks with a specific shape to it, most of it consumed by a single structural problem. The claims service still wrote every state change into a shared table designed in 2019, when Vachan had four customers and one line of business. Motor intake would add eleven new event types to that table, and the table already carried locking problems that produced two production incidents a month.

What Meera decided in that room would set the pattern for the rest of the year. If she carried the six-week date back to engineering as an instruction, she would get a version of it: something shipped, something hidden, and a squad that stopped telling her about risk because telling her had stopped changing anything. If she carried the fourteen-week estimate back to the customer as a fact, she would be treated — fairly — as a post office rather than a product manager, and the renewal conversation in November would be harder than it needed to be. The interesting move was neither. It required her to understand what the relationship between a product manager and an engineering team is actually for.

2 The idea, defined

The PM–engineering relationship is a standing exchange of two scarce goods. The product manager holds information about the world outside the building — which customer is unhappy, what the sales pipeline depends on, which regulator is watching, what a user actually does at 9 p.m. on a Sunday. The engineering team holds information about the inside of the system — what is load-bearing, what is rotten, what the true cost of each option is, and how wrong an estimate could be. Neither side can make a good decision alone, because a good decision requires both kinds of information at once. The relationship is the mechanism by which each side reliably gets what the other knows, early enough for it to matter.

Two terms, defined here because both are used loosely. Context means the reasoning behind a request — who has the problem, what it costs them, what would count as solved — as opposed to the request itself. Constraint disclosure means engineering telling the product manager the shape of the cost before a decision is taken, including the costs that are invisible from outside, such as a piece of the system that will need rewriting whether or not this feature ships.

The problem the relationship was invented to solve is old. When Neil McElroy wrote his memo at Procter & Gamble in 1931 proposing "brand men" who would own a product end to end, he was solving a coordination problem in a company where nobody was accountable for a brand as a whole. The software version has a more specific ancestry: Microsoft's program manager role, created in the late 1980s around the Excel team, was explicitly designed so that someone other than the engineering lead would own what the product should do, without owning how it was built. The Agile Manifesto in 2001 pushed the same division closer together in time — daily rather than quarterly — and by the mid-2000s the "two-in-a-box" pairing of a product manager and an engineering lead with equal standing had become the default shape at most large software companies. The division of labour is stable across all of it; the tempo is what has changed.

The sentence Meera could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib: "I own the problem and who has it. You own how it gets built and how long that takes. We decide the trade together, and neither of us is allowed to be surprised."

3 How the exchange actually works

Written as a list of obligations, the exchange is unromantic and quite short. It is worth setting out in full, because most of what goes wrong is a missing item rather than a missing virtue.

Read the left column carefully and notice what it is doing. Every item exists so that an engineer can decide something alone, correctly, at 4 p.m. on a Thursday when Meera is in a customer meeting. "The problem, not the solution" matters because an engineer who knows that a claims assessor is retyping a vehicle registration number from a photograph will propose three ways to remove the retyping, one of which Meera would never have thought of. An engineer who is handed "add a registration-number field with auto-capitalisation" will build exactly that and nothing better.

"The acceptable failure" is the item most often left implicit, and the most valuable. It is the answer to a question engineers ask constantly and product managers rarely answer in advance: if we cannot have everything, what may we drop, and who will be annoyed? At Vachan, Meera had never stated that the insurer's claims assessors mattered more than its regional managers, so every trade-off had come back up to her as a question, and each round trip cost a day.

On the right side, the item that separates a mature engineering team from a compliant one is the sixth: proposing the cheaper thing nobody asked for. When Arjun's team worked out that eighty per cent of the motor-intake value came from document upload and structured validation, and only twenty per cent from the historic-claims view, they were doing product work. The relationship is healthy precisely when both columns leak into each other a little.

4 A worked example: where fourteen weeks comes from

Arjun's fourteen weeks was not a feeling. Vachan's claims squad had nine engineers on two-week sprints. Ten working days per sprint, minus standing meetings, interviews and context-switching, left roughly 6.5 productive days per engineer per sprint — 58.5 engineer-days of raw capacity. Production support for existing insurers was consuming 36 per cent of that: 21 engineer-days a sprint, leaving 37.5 engineer-days of usable project capacity. That number, not headcount, is the one that governs everything.

Capacity: 58.5 engineer-days per sprint gross; 37.5 net of production support at 36 per cent. Base scope 292 ÷ 37.5 ≈ 7.8 sprints ≈ 15.6 weeks. Arjun's fourteen-week figure assumed support would fall to 25 per cent — an assumption nobody had written down.

Work the arithmetic through slowly, because the shape of it is the lesson. At 37.5 usable engineer-days a sprint, 292 engineer-days is 7.8 sprints, or a little under sixteen weeks. Arjun had quoted fourteen, which quietly assumed production support would drop from 36 per cent to 25 per cent — 44 usable days a sprint — because two long-running incidents were expected to close. That assumption was doing three weeks of work in the estimate and nobody had said it out loud. This is the single most common hidden ingredient in an estimate: not padding, but an unstated belief about the world.

Now change one input. Suppose the insurer agrees that for the first six months, historic claims can be read from the existing store rather than migrated. That one concession collapses two lines. The 96-day rewrite becomes a 22-day write-through adapter that sends new motor events to a new store while leaving the old table alone; the 30-day backfill disappears entirely. Total drops from 292 to 188. Change a second input — ship three of the eleven insurer-specific rule types now and configure the remaining eight by hand for the first quarter — and 52 becomes 18. Total: 154 engineer-days.

At 37.5 engineer-days a sprint, 154 days is 4.1 sprints — about 8.2 weeks. Still not six. The third move is different in kind: Arjun proposed rotating a dedicated on-call engineer and asking two non-critical insurers to accept a five-day rather than two-day response window for one quarter, which would cut support load from 36 per cent to roughly 21 per cent and lift usable capacity to 46 engineer-days a sprint. Then 154 ÷ 46 = 3.35 sprints, or 6.7 weeks — near enough that a go-live in the first week of the new financial year becomes an honest conversation rather than a hope.

Notice who owns each move. The first two are Meera's, because each one spends a specific customer's goodwill. The third is Arjun's, because it spends engineering's own slack. Neither could have produced the plan alone, and neither could have produced it at all if the estimate had arrived as a single number with no decomposition.

5 Seven nuances that separate understanding from vocabulary

An estimate is a distribution, and a date is a decision

"Fourteen weeks" is not a fact about the world; it is a point on a curve, usually somewhere near the median. A team that says "eight weeks at even odds, thirteen weeks at four-in-five odds, and the thing that would narrow the range is two days spent proving the adapter works" has told you something you can act on. A team that says "fourteen weeks" has told you a number you will later treat as a promise and they will later treat as an estimate. The product manager who asks only for the number, and never for the spread or the thing that would narrow it, has chosen comfort over information.

A technical objection is not a technical veto

Engineers raise two quite different kinds of "no", and conflating them poisons the relationship in both directions. A technical objection says this is more expensive than you think — it is priced information, and the product manager may legitimately decide to pay. A technical veto says this will corrupt data, breach the contract we signed, or create a failure we cannot recover from — it is not priced, and overriding it is a decision to accept a risk that the person overriding usually does not understand. Meera's discipline was to ask, every time: "Is this expensive, or is this unsafe?" The question is not rude, and a good engineer welcomes it, because it lets them spend their hard "no" where it counts.

Prioritisation is the PM's; sequencing inside a release is usually not

Which problems the team works on, and in what order of importance, is a product decision. The order in which work is actually undertaken within a chosen scope is frequently an engineering decision, because it depends on dependency structure, who is free, and where the risk sits. A product manager who reorders a sprint board because a stakeholder asked has usually crossed from the first into the second, and will be resented for it without quite understanding why.

Trust accrues in the small, boring decisions

The relationship is not built in the dramatic moment when a launch date is defended. It is built in the ordinary sprint where the product manager says: take the two days to fix the locking problem, I will explain the slip to sales myself. Vachan's squad had watched Meera do exactly this twice in the previous year, which is the only reason Arjun brought her a decomposed estimate rather than a defensive one. Reciprocity of this kind is slow to build and very fast to spend.

"Being technical enough" is the wrong target

Product managers are routinely told they must be technical to earn engineering's respect. What engineers actually need is a partner who can hold a trade-off in their head, ask a precise question, and not change the answer three days later. Depth helps — Meera knew what a write-through adapter was, and that saved an hour — but it is a lubricant, not the mechanism. Many technically fluent product managers are disliked, because fluency without restraint turns into design-by-PM.

Agile ceremony is not the relationship

A team can run immaculate stand-ups, refinement sessions and retrospectives and still have a broken relationship, because ceremony regulates tempo rather than information. The best product programmes teach this module through role-play and by putting an engineering partner in the room during design critiques, and they deliberately go light on agile mechanics — precisely because the mechanics are easy to teach, easy to perform, and easily mistaken for the substance. If the ceremonies are healthy and the relationship is not, you will see it in the questions that do not get asked in refinement.

What the relationship cannot do

However well it runs, the relationship cannot tell you whether the architecture is right, whether the market wants the product, or whether an estimate is honest. It cannot make a weak strategy work. What it can do is make concealment expensive and surprise rare — which is not the same thing as making decisions correct. A product manager who believes a strong engineering relationship is evidence of a good product is confusing a healthy circulatory system with a healthy patient.

6 How it shifts by product type and company stage

In consumer products the loop is short and the evidence is cheap: an engineer can ship a change to two per cent of users on Tuesday and both sides can read the result on Friday. Here the risk is that the product manager becomes a throughput manager, feeding the team a stream of small experiments with no accumulated argument, and engineers slowly disengage because nothing they build lasts.

In B2B and enterprise software, of which Vachan is a case, the loop is long and the evidence is thin: one insurer's opinion arrives loudly and is mistaken for the market's. Here the product manager's central obligation shifts to filtering — deciding which of eleven customer-specific rule types are genuinely product and which are configuration — and engineering's central obligation shifts to making the difference cheap, which is a design decision, not a project decision.

In marketplaces, no single request is ever from "the customer", because there are at least two customers with opposed interests; the relationship's hardest work is deciding which side's pain is being solved this quarter, and engineering needs that stated explicitly, because a change that helps sellers usually costs buyers something.

Stage changes the failure mode more than the principle. In a twenty-person company the two roles are separated by a desk, context flows by osmosis, and the risk is that nothing is written down, so the reasoning dies when the third engineer leaves. In a two-thousand-person company the risk inverts: everything is written down and nothing is read, the product manager is three levels away from the customer and the engineer is two levels away from the product manager, and the whole exchange degrades into ticket-passing unless someone insists on direct contact.

7 Four failure patterns and the cheapest test for each

The first is solutioned tickets. The symptom, visible from outside, is a refinement session in which engineers ask no questions — not because everything is clear, but because there is nothing to ask about a specification that has already decided everything. The underlying misunderstanding is that precision and completeness are the same thing. The cheapest diagnostic costs thirty seconds: ask an engineer on the team to state, in their own words, what problem the current sprint is solving and for whom. If you get the feature name back, the context never arrived.

The second is deadline laundering: a date the product manager chose is presented as a date the customer or the board imposed. The symptom is that the date never moves even when scope changes dramatically, and that no one can say what happens the day after it. The misunderstanding is that urgency is a substitute for priority. The diagnostic is a single question asked out loud: "What actually happens on the following Monday if we are a week late?" A real deadline has a crisp answer — a regulatory filing, a contractual penalty, a financial year boundary. A laundered one produces vagueness.

The third is silent debt trades. The symptom is that velocity is fine for two quarters and then collapses for no visible reason. The misunderstanding is on both sides: engineering assumes the product manager does not want to hear about shortcuts, and the product manager assumes that unmentioned shortcuts were not taken. The diagnostic is to ask, at every release, what was traded away to hit it and when the bill arrives. Vachan's 2019 claims table was exactly this: a sensible shortcut taken under pressure, never priced, now costing 96 engineer-days.

The fourth is the product manager as sole channel. The symptom is that every question about a user has to go through one person, and that person is a bottleneck with a full calendar. The misunderstanding is that owning the customer relationship means monopolising it. The diagnostic is a count: how many engineers on this squad have watched a real user work in the last eight weeks? At Vachan the answer in January was zero; by April, Arjun's engineers had sat with claims assessors twice, and the quality of their proposals changed noticeably.

8 What good looks like

Handled well, the same February meeting looks unremarkable. The product manager arrives with the problem and the stakes rather than the date: an insurer with a ₹4.2 crore contract needs motor intake before the financial year turns, and here is what their assessors do today. The engineering manager arrives with a decomposed estimate, its uncertainty, and the assumption it rests on, stated aloud. Together they find that two-thirds of the cost sits in work the customer does not value directly, and they test whether the customer will trade it. The product manager leaves with two concessions to negotiate; the engineering manager leaves with one capacity change to make. Nobody has been heroic. Nobody has been overruled. The commitment that goes to the customer is conditional and specific, and everyone in the room could recite the conditions a month later.

9 What Meera decided

Meera did not carry either number. She went back to the insurer's chief operating officer on 13 February with a proposal in three parts: motor intake live in the first week of the financial year, with three of the eleven rule types automated and the remaining eight configured by Vachan's team at no cost for one quarter; historic claims viewable through the existing screens, with migration completed by September; and a five-day support response window for two of Vachan's smaller accounts during the build, which she negotiated separately. The insurer accepted two of the three immediately and argued for a week about the rules.

Her reasoning was that the only genuinely fixed thing in the room was the financial-year boundary, and that everything else — scope, sequence, support posture — was negotiable if someone was willing to name its price. Engineering had given her the prices. Her job was to spend them in the right order.

What to read next follows directly. How PMs alienate engineers takes the failure patterns above and examines them from the other side of the table, where they are experienced as disrespect rather than as process error. Giving feedback on implementations addresses the moment this page has deliberately skipped — what happens when the thing gets built and the product manager does not like it, which is where more relationships are damaged than in any estimate conversation. Beyond those, engineering estimates and T-shirt sizing gives the formal treatment of the uncertainty question raised above.

Two questions to sit with.

First: in the last quarter, what did your engineering team tell you that you did not want to hear, and what did you visibly do about it? If nothing comes to mind, consider the possibility that the channel is closed rather than that the news was good.

Second: if you had to write down the "acceptable failure" for the work your team is doing right now — what may be dropped, and which specific person will be annoyed — could you do it in one sentence today, without asking anyone? If not, your team is making that call for you, several times a week, without the information you hold.

Tamhini Technologies: Two Truths About Amboli

An ambiguous case on the product manager–engineering relationship

Tamhini Technologies, its clients, its employees and the supervisory circular described here are fictional, invented for teaching. The market and institutions around them are real; no real company or person is portrayed.

1. Sunday night, Indiranagar

At twenty past eleven on Sunday, 11 October 2026, Shalaka Patwardhan sat on the floor of her flat in Indiranagar, Bengaluru, with two printouts side by side on the coffee table and an unopened suitcase behind her. The 6:20 flight would reach the investor’s office at Nariman Point, Mumbai, by noon; the technology committee of Tamhini Technologies’ board met at four. As Senior Director of Product she owned the decisioning platform that thirty-eight Indian lenders used to approve or decline some three crore credit applications a month, and she had been asked for one thing: a dated, costed, defensible plan to make every one of those decisions auditable in the form the Reserve Bank of India now required, by 31 January 2027.

The two printouts did not agree. The first, prepared by her own group product manager, showed the Amboli programme — Tamhini’s two-and-a-half-year rewrite of its credit-decisioning core — at sixty-three per cent complete, velocity at an all-time high, on course to absorb the regulatory work by December. The second, sent at 1:14 that morning by the head of platform engineering in Pune, showed Amboli carrying four per cent of live traffic, mismatching the old system on roughly one decision in nine hundred, and no closer to production readiness than in April. Both came from Tamhini’s own systems, from people she trusted. She had spent the weekend trying to work out not which was right, but how her organisation had held two irreconcilable beliefs about the same software for fourteen months without either being tested.

What she would have to say in Mumbai was harder still. The committee would not ask about story points. It would ask whether Tamhini could certify compliance to its clients by 31 January, what that would cost, and why the programme the board had funded with ₹22 crore was not simply the answer.

2. How Tamhini got here

Tamhini Technologies Private Limited was founded in 2015 in Pune by three engineers who had spent a decade building core banking integrations for large Indian lenders. Their first product, a decisioning engine known internally as Purandar, did something unglamorous and valuable: it took an application from a lender’s app or branch, pulled bureau data, income signals and policy rules, and returned an approve, decline or refer decision fast enough that the borrower never saw a spinner. By 2018 it was live at two NBFCs; by 2020, at eleven.

The decision that shaped everything afterwards was taken in 2021. Flush with a Series B, the founders moved the headquarters and all new product development to Bengaluru, where the talent market was deeper. Purandar, the monolith, stayed in Pune with the engineers who had written it. The stated logic was clean: Pune would keep the lights on, Bengaluru would build the next generation. The unstated consequence was that Tamhini’s architecture and its org chart began to mirror each other, and then to defend each other. Pune owned reliability and knew where every undocumented rule was buried. Bengaluru owned the future and the founders’ attention.

In 2023 the company hired a chief product officer from a large enterprise-software firm, who brought an operating model with him: quarterly planning increments, cross-functional squads, and a clean division in which product owned what and why and engineering owned how. It was a professionalising move, and it worked for a while. It also created a habit: because the ritual layer produced numbers — committed points, accepted stories, confidence votes — leadership increasingly read those numbers instead of talking to engineers. Product managers stopped sitting in architecture reviews, because architecture was how. Engineers stopped arguing about scope, because scope was what.

In March 2024 the board approved Amboli: an eighteen-month, ₹22 crore programme to replace Purandar with a modular, multi-entity decisioning core, sponsored by chief architect Devdatt Iyer and staffed out of a new Hyderabad office. Eighteen months became thirty; by September 2026, ₹31.4 crore had been spent.

3. The industry

Tamhini sells into one of the most heavily supervised technology markets in the world. Its clients are NBFCs, small finance banks and the digital-lending arms of private banks; its competitors include Lentra, Perfios, Signzy and M2P Fintech, alongside the in-house platform teams large lenders periodically decide to build and periodically decide to stop building. Its plumbing runs through public infrastructure it does not control: the Account Aggregator framework, CKYC and CERSAI, the bureaus — TransUnion CIBIL, Experian, CRIF — NPCI’s rails for disbursement and repayment, and the credit-line-on-UPI flows that have pushed latency budgets from seconds to tens of milliseconds. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act governs what may be stored, mirrored and shown to whom; ONDC’s credit protocol promises a further wave of volume and of scrutiny.

The proximate cause of Shalaka’s weekend was a supervisory circular issued on 14 July 2026, extending the Reserve Bank’s digital-lending framework. In substance it required that every automated credit decision be reconstructible — rule and model versions, input data and consent artefacts, decision path, any human override — and exported to the lender in machine-readable form. The regulated entities are accountable, but they cannot comply unless their technology service providers do, and Tamhini is that provider for thirty-eight of them. Compliance date: 31 January 2027.

Since 2025 Tamhini has also sold into the Gulf, where the Central Bank of the UAE’s open-finance programme and the Al Etihad Credit Bureau have created a comparable modernisation wave. Its largest international contract, ₹9.6 crore over three years with Al Sadara Finance in Dubai, requires a March 2027 go-live with multi-entity, multi-currency support that Purandar has never had and cannot plausibly be retrofitted with. Only Amboli was designed for it.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

Amboli began with a defensible thesis. Purandar was eleven years old, written in a mixture of Java and stored procedures, with policy logic in three places and an audit trail that recorded outcomes but not reasoning. Rewriting it would take eighteen months, after which international expansion, model governance and regulatory reporting would all be easier. Until June 2025 the programme shipped its internal milestones on schedule as measured by module acceptance. In July 2025 it slipped by four months; in January 2026, by five more. Each slip was explained by scope discovered rather than added, and each explanation was accepted, because the delivery dashboard kept showing an upward line (Exhibit 2).

In January 2026 Amboli took its first production traffic: two per cent of applications at one mid-sized NBFC, Purandar running in parallel and arbitrating. By September it was at four per cent (Exhibit 3). Devdatt called this deliberate caution. Ranjeet Salunke, who runs platform engineering in Pune, called it, in a message to Shalaka, “the only number here that has not been marketed at you.”

When the circular landed in July, Tamhini had to tell its clients something. Nilofer Qureshi, the compliance director in Mumbai, drafted a letter; Harish Menon, managing director for international markets, pressed for a confident version; the chief executive signed it on 6 August. It promised full compliance “on the new decisioning platform, by 31 January 2027.” Nobody had asked engineering for an estimate. They had asked for the dashboard, and the dashboard said sixty-one per cent.

Three things have since turned out to be wrong. First, the sixty-three per cent counts modules accepted against a baseline revised twice, each revision removing work rather than adding it; against the March 2024 baseline the same modules are forty-one per cent. Second, a shadow test in the first week of September, running five per cent of live traffic through both cores, produced 1,140 decision mismatches, of which Devdatt’s team classified 900 as “expected differences arising from improved policy logic” — a classification made by the team that wrote the new logic, reviewed by nobody outside it. Third, the assumption that Purandar could not produce a compliant audit trail is no longer safe. On 28 September, Ranjeet sent Shalaka a working prototype: a decision-journal service writing an immutable, versioned record out of Purandar, built over six weeks by four Pune engineers in time nobody had allocated, covering, he claimed, seventy per cent of the circular’s requirements. He had told no one he was building it. He had tested it by replaying eleven months of production decision data into staging — which Nilofer, told of it on Friday, said she would have to review very carefully under the DPDP Act.

A fourth thing is unsettled. An industry-association clarification circulated on 2 October suggests the requirement extends to manual overrides by lenders’ credit officers, not only to automated decisions. If that reading holds, every option grows: override capture is a Purandar-side workflow Amboli has never scoped. Nobody at Tamhini has read the clarification with counsel.

5. The people

Shalaka Patwardhan — Senior Director, Product, Bengaluru

Four years at Tamhini, previously a product manager at a payments company. She owns the decisioning platform’s roadmap and is accountable to the board for the compliance date. Her position is that she needs one technical truth before she can plan anything. Her incentive is a promotion the chief executive has tied to “landing the regulatory programme cleanly.” What she is not saying: she cannot personally evaluate either Devdatt’s or Ranjeet’s claims, has never asked to sit in an Amboli design review, and suspects the operating model she has enforced for three years is the reason she has no way of knowing.

Devdatt Iyer — Chief Architect and Amboli sponsor, Hyderabad

Joined in 2021 from a global product company; built the Hyderabad office to thirty-four engineers, most recruited personally. His position is that stopping Amboli now would waste ₹31 crore and leave Tamhini with a core that cannot support international clients, model governance, or the next circular. His incentive is that Amboli is his: his standing, his office and his team’s equity narrative are attached to it. What he is not saying: two of his four senior engineers have told him privately that the decision-orchestration module needs redesigning, and he has put that in writing nowhere.

Ranjeet Salunke — Head of Platform Engineering, Pune

Eight years at Tamhini, one of the original Purandar authors. His position is that Purandar is not a legacy embarrassment but a system that returns a decision in forty-eight milliseconds at the ninety-ninth percentile, and that compliance is nine to fourteen weeks of honest work on it. His incentive is survival: since 2021 his team has been described in every all-hands as maintenance. What he is not saying: he built the prototype partly to prove a point, he knows the DPDP question about the replayed data is real, and three of his best engineers have told him of offers elsewhere, which he has not escalated.

Tarun Ghai — Group Product Manager, Amboli, Bengaluru

Shalaka’s direct report, two years in role, author of the delivery dashboard. His position is that the programme is measurable and on track and that Pune’s numbers are anecdotes. His incentive is a quarterly rating computed from programme burn-up and predictability. What he is not saying: he authorised both baseline revisions himself, believing them scope clarifications, and has never seen the production traffic figures, which sit in an engineering dashboard he cannot access.

Nilofer Qureshi — Director, Compliance and Risk, Mumbai

Ex-regulator, joined 2024. Her position is that the 31 January date is immovable and that she will not sign a certification she cannot evidence. Her incentive is personal: her name goes on the client attestations. What she is not saying: she drafted the August client letter from the dashboard, knows it, and has not told the board that the letter was written without an engineering estimate.

Harish Menon — Managing Director, International, Singapore

Hired in 2024 to build the Gulf and South-East Asia business; carries a ₹40 crore three-year target. His position is that Amboli must not slow down, because Al Sadara’s March 2027 go-live and two further UAE prospects depend on capabilities only Amboli has. His incentive is his own P&L and a variable component weighted to international bookings. What he is not saying: Al Sadara’s chief technology officer asked him in September whether the new platform was running anywhere at scale, and he answered that it was “in production with Indian clients” — true only in the sense Exhibit 3 makes clear.

Anneke de Vries — Head of Design, Amsterdam

Leads a four-person design team across two time zones. Her position is that the client-facing artefact of this programme is the lender console — what a credit officer sees when a decision must be explained to a regulator — and that it has been redesigned twice and shipped never, because nobody will say which core it sits on. Her incentive is keeping her small team from disintegrating. What she is not saying: two of her four designers have asked to move elsewhere in the business.

Sudeep Nanda — Board observer, Series C investor, Mumbai

Sits on the technology committee. His position is that Tamhini must reach profitability by FY28 and that running two cores in parallel is an indefensible cost. His incentive is his fund’s mark and an exit window. What he is not saying: his fund’s thesis referenced the new platform explicitly, so a public retreat from Amboli would be awkward for him as well as for Devdatt.

B. Comply on Purandar and slow Amboli

Cheapest, fastest, and it rewards the team carrying the traffic. Shalaka drafted these three on Saturday and disliked all of them by Sunday, without being able to say why. Each is a question about architecture and money. The compliance date of 31 January 2027 is not a Tamhini date and cannot be renegotiated with a client. Three of the top five contracts carry regulatory pass-through clauses worth up to fifteen per cent of annual fees in service credits, an exposure of about ₹4.3 crore, and one carries a termination-for-convenience right that activates on a compliance failure; that client is ₹11.8 crore of ₹168 crore FY26 revenue. Al Sadara carries ₹40 lakh a month, capped at ₹2 crore, for a go-live later than March 2027.

The investor has imposed a headcount freeze through FY27; new engineers must be contractors, at roughly ₹2.4 lakh per engineer-month, and Devdatt has said publicly that contractors cannot be productive on Amboli in under ten weeks. Ranjeet has three engineers with live offers. The committee has scheduled ninety minutes, of which Shalaka has twenty.

  1. Reading Exhibits 2 and 3 together, what is actually known about Amboli’s readiness, and what is merely asserted? Which single piece of evidence, if Shalaka could obtain it by Friday, would most change her plan?
  2. Why did Tamhini’s product organisation come to believe Exhibit 2? Trace the mechanism — not the intent — by which a set of honest numbers produced a false picture, and identify who could have interrupted it.
  3. Ranjeet built something significant without being asked, in time nobody allocated, and did not tell anyone. Is that a success of engineering initiative or a failure of the working relationship? What would have had to be true for that work to happen in the open?
  4. What do Devdatt, Ranjeet, Anneke and Tarun each need from Shalaka that they are not getting — and what does Shalaka need from each of them that she has never explicitly asked for? Where do those two lists conflict?
  5. The 2023 operating model gave product the what and engineering the how. Evaluate that boundary against the evidence in this case. If you would redraw it, say precisely what moves and who would object; if you would keep it, explain how Exhibits 2 and 3 could have been reconciled within it.
  6. It is Monday, 12 October. Shalaka has twenty minutes with the board’s technology committee. What does she do first thing that morning, what does she say in those twenty minutes about the 31 January date, and what does she commit to that she can actually keep?

11. Late

Just before midnight Shalaka opened the document where the three options sat, and instead of editing them she typed a fourth heading — “What we will do differently after this” — and looked at it for a long time. Then she deleted it, unable to decide whether it was the most important thing she would say in Mumbai or the surest way to lose the room. Her phone showed a message from Ranjeet at 23:51: whatever you decide, tell us on Monday itself, the team is asking. Nine minutes later, one from Devdatt: call me before you present. There is something about the orchestration module you should hear from me and not from the dashboard. She had a 4:30 alarm set and no idea what she was going to say.

Malvan Systems: The White Friday Decision

A short decision case on the product manager–engineering relationship

Tuesday, 15 September 2026, half past nine in the evening, Kalyani Nagar, Pune. Kunal Bhosale, Director of Product at Malvan Systems, was still at his desk on the fourth floor of the Amar Business Park tower, the office mostly dark except for three monitors and the glow of Bengaluru still on video two floors down. On Monday, 21 September, he would stand before Malvan’s executive steering committee — the two co-founders, the head of sales, and the board observer from the Series B investor — and tell them whether Malvan would hit its 20 November commitment to Al Wafra Hypermarkets, the company’s first large Gulf client, in time for White Friday, the UAE’s biggest shopping weekend. He had until Friday evening to decide not just the answer, but how he would get there: by pushing engineering harder, the way he had for six weeks, or by changing, fundamentally, how he worked with them.

1. The company

Malvan Systems Private Limited was founded in 2018 in Pune by two engineers who had met at IIT Bombay and spent their first careers building warehouse software for a logistics arm of a large retail group. Their product, OrderTide, sat between a direct-to-consumer brand’s storefront and its warehouses, couriers and return centres, orchestrating which order shipped from where and, increasingly, managing the costly business of reverse logistics — the returns, exchanges and refunds that ate into every D2C brand’s margin. Malvan’s customers were brands that had grown fast on Indian e-commerce but could not justify building this plumbing themselves: skincare labels in the Mamaearth mould, eyewear players comparable to Lenskart, and apparel brands selling through Flipkart, Myntra and the ONDC network. Malvan did not compete with the quick-commerce giants — Zepto, Blinkit and Swiggy Instamart ran their own dark-store logistics end to end — but it competed hard against Unicommerce and Increff, established Indian players in the same category, and against every founder’s instinct to build the capability in-house.

By September 2026, Malvan employed 240 people and had crossed ₹38 crore in annual recurring revenue, having raised a Series B round eighteen months earlier to fund expansion beyond India. Its engineering organisation numbered 64: forty in Bengaluru, around checkout and fulfilment, and twenty-four in Pune, who owned returns, refunds and fraud-and-abuse detection. Product design sat with a single lead designer, Lukas Weber, in Berlin. A two-person data science function reported to Kunal from Toronto, led by Priya Subramaniam. Customer success ran from Singapore under Mei-Ling Tan, and enterprise sales was led by Neil Fernandes, from New Jersey, near Malvan’s US prospects and its first Gulf deal.

2. The situation

Six months earlier, in March 2026, Neil had closed a three-year, ₹4.2 crore contract with Al Wafra Hypermarkets, a large Gulf retail chain looking to modernise its online returns experience ahead of White Friday, the Emirati adaptation of Black Friday anchoring the UAE’s November retail calendar. The contract carried a specific milestone: a new returns and fraud-screening flow, live and load-tested, by 20 November. Neil had negotiated the date directly with Al Wafra’s Dubai operations team without a detailed estimate from engineering, reasoning — correctly, in isolation — that Malvan could not afford to lose its first anchor account outside India over a scheduling conversation.

Kunal had absorbed that date as a fact rather than a negotiation, and had responded the way he usually did under pressure: by writing detailed specifications himself and handing them to engineering as tickets, spelling out not just what the returns flow needed to do but how the screens should behave and which APIs to call in which order. It felt like the fastest way to move: no time lost explaining context, no risk of engineers designing something off-brief. For the first four sprints it seemed to work. By sprint six it had stopped working. Arvind Rao, who led the Bengaluru engineering group, had asked for thirty minutes with Kunal that afternoon and had been blunt: the team was implementing his specifications faster than it could question them, several did not account for how the existing fraud pipeline behaved under load, and two resulting defects had already reached production, one of which had incorrectly frozen refunds for eleven Al Wafra pilot customers over Eid al-Etihad weekend before anyone caught it.

From Bengaluru, Arvind saw a team that had stopped being consulted and started merely executing, pulled off design reviews to keep pace with tickets that arrived fully formed. From Pune, the returns squad was quietly accumulating technical debt in the fraud module. From Toronto, Priya had been asking for three uninterrupted weeks to rebuild the data pipeline the fraud model depended on — complicated by the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, since Al Wafra’s customer data could not simply be mirrored to Toronto without a compliant transfer design — and had been told each sprint it was not yet the priority. From Berlin, Lukas’s redesigned returns flow, tested in August, sat shelved for six weeks because Kunal had gone straight to tickets to save a review cycle. Mei-Ling in Singapore reported the client still confident but now twice asking for a demo rather than a slide.

3. The people

Arvind Rao — VP Engineering, Bengaluru

Arvind had joined Malvan from a fintech scale-up and built the Bengaluru team from nine engineers to forty. He was not opposed to the White Friday date; he was opposed to being handed finished decisions. He wanted to be pulled into scoping before specifications were written, not after, and the freedom to flag a technically expensive idea before it became a committed date. He had told his own team, more than once, that he would not let Malvan repeat the Eid weekend incident.

Neil Fernandes — Head of Enterprise Sales, New Jersey

Neil had built his year around the Al Wafra account and had a second, larger Gulf prospect waiting to see Malvan deliver on time before signing. He wanted the 20 November date held exactly as promised, viewed slippage as a credibility problem for Malvan’s whole Gulf ambition, and was, by his own admission, unqualified to judge whether the date was technically realistic.

Priya Subramaniam — Data Science Lead, Toronto

Priya wanted three protected weeks to rebuild the fraud-pipeline foundation before further feature work landed on top of it, treated as a dependency the launch plan was built around, not a nice-to-have competing sprint by sprint with everything else.

Fatima Al Naqbi — VP Operations, Al Wafra Hypermarkets, Dubai

Fatima wanted a working, reliable returns experience live for White Friday traffic, and had told Mei-Ling plainly that a phased rollout she trusted mattered more than a big-bang date she did not.

Exhibit 1 shows what Arvind had brought to the meeting: delivered points falling as planned points held roughly steady, unplanned work climbing from 12 to 41 percent of capacity, and overtime more than tripling across six sprints — a team absorbing scope shocks rather than doing planned work. Exhibit 2 shows why Neil’s instinct to protect the date was not unreasonable on its own terms: the milestone payment, the capped but real penalty, and the second Gulf prospect watching from the sidelines. It also shows the cost of a second incident, in support effort, credits and Fatima’s confidence, could exceed the cost of resourcing the work properly now. 5. The options

Option A: Hold the date, add capacity, keep driving from the top

Kunal could bring in the two contract engineers already quoted at ₹18 lakh, keep writing detailed specifications himself to avoid losing time to onboarding, and ask Arvind’s team to sustain the current pace through November. The upside was speed and certainty for Neil and Fatima: the date protected, as promised. The cost was that it treated the Eid incident as a capacity problem rather than a process problem; Exhibit 1’s trend suggested adding hands to a team already drowning in unplanned work and specification handoffs, without changing how work reached them, risked a second and larger failure at the worst possible moment.

Option B: Renegotiate scope with Al Wafra and rebuild the working relationship with engineering

Kunal could ask Mei-Ling to arrange a call with Fatima to propose a phased launch: a simpler, thoroughly tested core returns flow live by 20 November, with the fraud-screening layer that caused the Eid incident following six weeks later once Priya’s pipeline work was done properly. In parallel, Kunal would bring Arvind, Priya and Lukas into scoping the remaining eight weeks this week, replacing his specifications with stated outcomes and constraints and letting engineering own the how. The upside was a launch on a stable foundation and a reset relationship with the people building it. The cost was an uncomfortable conversation with Neil, a real risk Fatima says no, and Kunal admitting his own working style had contributed to the problem.

Option C: Escalate and create a parallel delivery track

Kunal could ask the co-founders to approve a dedicated six-person pod, pulled from elsewhere at roughly ₹42 lakh over ten weeks, to take over the Al Wafra work while Arvind’s team returned to its normal roadmap. The upside was isolating the crisis without asking Al Wafra for anything or changing how Kunal worked day to day. The cost was the highest of the three in cash terms, it pulled experienced engineers off other committed work with its own stakeholders, and it did nothing to address why product and engineering had broken down in the first place, leaving the same dynamic free to recur.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. What does Exhibit 1 tell you about the actual source of Malvan’s delivery risk, and is it primarily a capacity problem, a scoping problem, or a relationship problem?
  2. Whose needs has Kunal been meeting for the past six sprints, and whose has he been ignoring? What would Arvind, Priya and Lukas each say they need from him that they are not currently getting?
  3. What has Kunal, as the product manager, specifically needed from engineering that he has not been asking for — and what would change if he asked for it?
  4. Given Exhibit 2’s numbers, which option best protects both the Al Wafra relationship and Malvan’s ability to deliver its next commitment reliably, not just this one?

7. A note for the learner

This case sits inside one question that recurs in every product manager’s working life: what do engineers need from me, and what do I need from them? Kunal’s trouble did not begin with the Al Wafra date — dates arrive from sales and clients in every company, and a competent PM absorbs and negotiates them constantly. It began when he answered time pressure by substituting his own detailed instructions for his engineers’ judgment: Arvind’s team stopped being consulted on feasibility, Priya’s well-founded request for foundational work kept losing to whatever ticket was most urgent, and Lukas’s tested design was discarded to save a review cycle that would have caught problems earlier than production did. Exhibit 1’s rising unplanned-work line is that pattern from the outside: a team perpetually reacting rather than building.

A well-reasoned answer does not simply pick the option kindest to engineering, nor the one safest for the client relationship; the two are, at this point, the same problem. Engineers need to be brought into scoping before commitments are made, not handed finished specifications after; they need protection from scope thrash once a sprint begins; and they need a PM who treats a flagged risk, like Priya’s request or Arvind’s warning, as information to act on, not noise to route around. In turn, the PM needs engineers to say plainly when a date is not credible, to surface risk early, and to trust that raising a concern will change the plan.

The most defensible path is Option B. It costs an uncomfortable conversation with Neil and a real risk Fatima says no, but Exhibit 2 shows a second incident’s exposure rivals the penalty for a short, well-managed delay, and Exhibit 1 shows the team cannot sustain Option A’s pace. Option C spends the most money to avoid the actual lesson. Phasing the launch, scoping the remaining work jointly, and giving engineering outcomes to own rather than instructions to follow treats the PM–engineering relationship as the foundation delivery sits on, not a resource managed around a deadline.

The PM–engineering relationship

An exchange of information under uncertainty — its intellectual history, its quantitative structure, its edge cases, and the disagreements the field has not settled.

1 Two rooms, two Marches

On 4 March, in a converted warehouse off Bannerghatta Road in Bengaluru, Rhea Menon was making an argument she had made twice before and lost. Rhea was group product manager for the shopping experience at Amrai Fresh, a grocery-delivery business running about 2.8 lakh orders a day across eleven cities, with forty engineers organised into six squads. The subject was substitutions: what the application offers a customer when a picker at a dark store finds the 500 g pack of curd they ordered is gone. Amrai's current behaviour was to remove the line and refund it. Roughly eleven per cent of orders lost at least one line this way, and internal analysis put the revenue leak at a little over ₹12 crore a year.

Kabir Dutt, Amrai's engineering director, was not disagreeing about the money. He was disagreeing about the path. Rhea wanted a personalised substitution model — given this customer's two-year purchase history, offer the replacement they are most likely to accept. Kabir's position was that the catalogue read path, which served substitution candidates, was already at 71 per cent of its provisioned capacity at the 7 p.m. peak, and that adding a per-customer lookup to it would require a nine-week rewrite before anything could ship at all. Rhea's experiment window closed with the quarter on 31 March. Nine weeks put the earliest learning into June.

Fifteen days later and four hundred kilometres south, Devika Iyer was in a different kind of room in Coimbatore. Kshipra Grid Systems built feeder-level metering hardware for electricity distribution utilities — a sealed box on a pole, and a cloud platform that turned its readings into loss-detection analytics for state discoms. Devika was the product manager for the platform. The next hardware revision, GX-4, had a firmware freeze on 30 April, and Devika wanted one thing in it: a field-configurable sampling rate, so that a utility could move a feeder from fifteen-minute to one-minute sampling without a site visit.

Kshipra's firmware lead, Suresh Palaniappan, put the cost at six weeks of engineering and validation, most of it validation, because anything touching the sampling loop had to be re-qualified against the accuracy class the boxes were certified to. Six weeks from 19 March landed after the freeze. And unlike Rhea's problem, Devika's had no second chance: a firmware defect shipped on 42,000 units a year is not rolled back with a feature flag. It is rolled back with a van.

The two rooms look like different problems. They are the same problem seen at different values of one variable — the cost of being wrong — and the argument of this page is that almost everything worth knowing about the product-manager-to-engineering relationship falls out of taking that variable seriously.

2 The idea, its history, and the schools that disagree

Define the relationship precisely, because loose definitions are the source of most of the confusion. The PM–engineering relationship is a standing bilateral exchange of private information under a division of decision rights. Each side holds information the other cannot cheaply obtain. The product manager holds information about the world outside the system: which customer is leaving, what a regulator will accept, what a user does at 9 p.m. on a Sunday, what the business will and will not fund. The engineering team holds information about the inside of the system: what is load-bearing, what is rotten, what each option really costs, and how wrong the cost estimate could be. The exchange exists so that decisions are taken with both halves of the information present. The division of decision rights exists so that the exchange terminates in an actual decision rather than in a permanent conversation.

Two definitions to fix as we go. Decision rights means who may decide a class of question without seeking agreement — distinct from who may be consulted, who may object, and who may escalate. Private information is used here in its economic sense: information one party holds that the other cannot verify at reasonable cost, which is what makes the relationship a trust problem rather than a process problem.

The lineage is longer than the software industry. Neil McElroy's 1931 memorandum at Procter & Gamble proposing "brand men" solved an accountability gap: nobody owned a brand end to end. The software form arrived with Microsoft's program manager role, created around the Excel team in the mid-1980s, which deliberately separated the person who decided what the product should do from the person who decided how it would be built — on the theory that fusing them produced either beautiful software nobody wanted or popular software nobody could maintain. Melvin Conway's 1968 observation that organisations ship their communication structure supplied the uncomfortable corollary: the relationship does not merely affect the product, it partly determines the architecture. The Agile Manifesto in 2001 compressed the exchange from quarterly to daily. Westrum's organisational typology, developed for aviation safety and later imported into software, supplied the causal claim that information flow — not structure, not process — is what distinguishes high-performing organisations from the rest; the DORA research programme published in Accelerate (2018) found the same variable at the top of its models. Basecamp's Shape Up (2019) and Skelton and Pais's Team Topologies (2019) represent the most recent serious attempts to formalise the division.

Practitioners who have thought hard about this divide into four camps that do not agree, and it is worth stating exactly what each would sign and refuse.

Exhibit 1 — Four schools, and the propositions each would and would not sign
SchoolWould signWould not signStrongest in
Separation of concerns
(program-manager lineage; empowered product teams)		 The PM owns value and viability, design owns usability, engineering owns feasibility; none overrides another's domain, and the team is given problems, not specifications. That a PM should ever specify implementation, or that a roadmap of features is a legitimate artefact. Consumer and B2B software with reversible releases
Engineering-led / fixed appetite
(Shape Up lineage; "product engineer" view)		 Appetite is fixed and scope is variable; the people building decide what gets built inside the appetite, and unshipped scope is not a failure. That an externally fixed backlog should determine what a team does in a cycle, or that estimates should be collected at all. Small teams, own-product companies, low external commitment
Specification / contract Ambiguity is the enemy; a versioned written specification with acceptance criteria and a change-control process is the relationship. That requirements should emerge during construction, or that a verbal agreement in a stand-up binds anyone. Regulated, hardware, safety-critical, outsourced
Relational / information-flow Information flow is the causal variable; role clarity and process are downstream, and a generative culture outperforms a well-specified one. That redrawing decision rights fixes a relationship, or that a RACI chart has ever changed a behaviour. Everywhere, as a diagnosis; nowhere, as a mechanism

The four are not mutually exclusive in practice, but they give different answers to concrete questions — who writes acceptance criteria, whether estimates should exist, whether scope may be cut without consultation — and a team that has never noticed it holds one of them will argue about the answers without discovering that it is arguing about the premise.

Note what the table implies about our two protagonists. Amrai Fresh sits squarely where the separation-of-concerns school is strongest: releases are reversible, experiments are cheap, and giving the squad a problem rather than a specification is plainly right. Kshipra sits where the specification school is strongest: the artefact is sealed, certified and physically distributed, and "we will figure out the details during the cycle" is not a sentence anyone can safely say about a sampling loop. A practitioner who has internalised only one school will handle one of these two rooms well and the other badly.

3 Mechanics in depth, with the arithmetic

Expert practitioners do three things that competent ones usually leave implicit: they price decision latency, they defend slack, and they audit the assumptions inside estimates. Each has a quantitative treatment.

Decision latency has a price, and it is computable

At Amrai, a fully-loaded engineer costs roughly ₹38 lakh a year, which over about 240 working days is ₹15,800 per engineer-day. Kabir's instrumentation of the squads' work-in-progress showed that, on average, eight engineers at any time were carrying an item blocked on a product decision, and that the mean block lasted 0.6 days. That is 4.8 engineer-days lost per week — ₹75,840 a week, or about ₹39 lakh a year, spent entirely on waiting for answers. It is roughly the cost of an additional senior engineer, and it is invisible in every budget because nobody books it.

The number matters less than what it licenses. Once a product manager can say "my response time costs us a headcount a year", the argument for keeping two hours a day unbooked stops being about personal preference and becomes a capital-allocation argument. The corresponding obligation on engineering is to make the blocks visible in the first place — an item that sits silently in progress for three days is a failure of disclosure, not of patience.

Slack is a product decision, and the maths is unforgiving

The most consequential second-order effect in this relationship is queueing. A team is a service system: work arrives, gets processed, departs. The standard single-server queueing result is that expected waiting time scales with ρ/(1−ρ), where ρ is utilisation — the fraction of capacity committed. The curve is not gentle. At 50 per cent utilisation the expected wait is one unit of service time; at 80 per cent it is four; at 90 per cent it is nine; at 95 per cent it is nineteen.

This is why "we have no capacity for that" and "we are fully booked" are not the same statement, and why an experienced engineering manager guards unbooked time with an intensity that looks, from the product side, like sandbagging. It is not sandbagging; it is the purchase of responsiveness. The expert product-management behaviour is to name the trade explicitly: at Amrai, Rhea and Kabir eventually agreed a standing 20 per cent unallocated band, and Rhea defended it in quarterly planning against her own incentives.

Estimates are distributions with an assumption audit attached

Suresh's six-week figure at Kshipra was, on examination, three separate estimates stacked: two weeks of firmware work with narrow uncertainty, one week of bench testing with narrow uncertainty, and three weeks of accuracy re-qualification with very wide uncertainty, because it depended on whether the external test house had a slot. Stated as a distribution rather than a number: a fifty-fifty chance of five weeks, a four-in-five chance of eight weeks, and a small but real chance of twelve if the test slot moved.

The expert move here is not to ask for a better number. It is to ask the question that converts uncertainty into a decision: what is the cheapest thing we could do in the next three days that would most narrow that range? At Kshipra the answer was a phone call to the test house to reserve a provisional slot — two hours of work that removed the twelve-week tail entirely. Most wide estimates contain one dominant source of variance, and it is frequently cheap to resolve, but only if someone asks.

4 When the standard division applies — and when it misleads

The separation-of-concerns model is usually presented as universal. It is not. It rests on four conditions, each of which can be stated as a testable claim and checked against a real team.

Claim one: the cost of reversing a wrong decision is low relative to the cost of deliberating about it. Test it by asking how long it takes to undo a shipped change and who is harmed in the interval. At Amrai the answer is minutes, behind a feature flag, harming a few thousand orders; the claim holds, and giving the squad a problem statement rather than a specification is the right call. At Kshipra the answer is a van, ₹2,900 a unit, and a utility's trust; the claim fails, and Devika must behave more like the specification school, writing down acceptance criteria and change control that would be absurd at Amrai.

Claim two: the team's cognitive load is bounded to one coherent domain. Test it by asking an engineer how many distinct systems they were paged about last month. Amrai's checkout squad passes; its platform squad, serving all six product squads, does not, and for that squad the standard model is quietly wrong — its customer is engineering, not a shopper, and a product manager who insists on framing its work in end-user terms will be politely ignored.

Claim three: the product manager controls the whole priority queue for the team. Test it by counting the people who can add work without the product manager's consent. Where the answer is more than one — a shared platform, a support escalation path, a security function — the relationship is not bilateral at all, and treating it as bilateral produces a product manager who is accountable for a queue they do not govern. This is the most common structural cause of a product manager being seen as ineffective, and it is not a skill problem.

Claim four: the exchange is symmetric in expertise. Where the technology is genuinely novel — an AI-native product being the current example — engineering cannot forecast quality, only effort, and the product manager cannot specify an outcome, only a threshold. Both sides lose their usual currency at once. The standard model is actively misleading here, because it encourages a product manager to ask for a commitment that no honest engineer can give.

5 Hard cases: seams, platforms, regulation, hardware, AI

Most of the genuinely difficult problems in this relationship do not occur inside a team. They occur at the seams between teams, where Conway's law does its work.

Mature companies handle this less elegantly than they say they do. The published answer is to give the platform team a product manager and an internal roadmap. The actual answer, in most organisations that work, is a monthly forum in which the three product managers argue in front of each other and someone senior arbitrates — slow, political, but at least placing the allocation decision with people who own business outcomes. What does not work, and is nonetheless common, is the escalation race, in which each product manager quietly lobbies the tech lead and the loudest wins.

Regulated and hardware contexts change the relationship in a specific way: they move the point of no return earlier. At Kshipra, everything is negotiable until 30 April and almost nothing afterwards, which means the exchange of information has a deadline that has nothing to do with the release date. Devika's obligation is therefore front-loaded — she must surface her requirement early enough to be validated, and the failure mode is not shipping late, it is discovering a requirement on 2 May. Mature hardware organisations institutionalise this with a formal requirements-freeze review; less mature ones rely on the product manager remembering.

Two-sided businesses add a different distortion. When a marketplace's engineers are told "the customer wants X", the honest question is which customer, and the product manager who cannot answer crisply has smuggled a strategy decision into a requirement. A change that speeds seller onboarding usually degrades buyer quality; engineering can often see the trade in the data model before the product manager sees it in the business.

AI-native products break the relationship's usual currency most severely. When Amrai's team later explored a language-model-based substitution explainer, the estimate question changed shape: the engineers could say confidently how long it would take to build the pipeline, and could say nothing at all about how long it would take to make the outputs good enough. The mature adaptation is to renegotiate what is being committed to. Instead of "ship the explainer by 30 June", the commitment becomes "by 30 June we will have an evaluation set of 400 labelled substitution cases and a measured acceptance rate; we commit to the measurement, not the number." Product managers who cannot make that shift will keep asking for dates and keep being given fiction.

6 Nine nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

The estimate you receive is a function of what happened to the last one

Estimates are not drawn from a distribution of beliefs; they are drawn from a distribution of beliefs conditioned on consequences. A team whose last honest estimate was negotiated down in public will pad the next one, and the padding will be invisible because it will be distributed across line items rather than added at the end. The tell-tale sign an expert watches for is uniformity: a decomposed estimate in which every item is suspiciously round and none is stated as a range has usually been pre-negotiated inside the team before it reached you.

An argument about an API boundary is usually an argument about ownership

Conway's law runs in both directions: the organisation shapes the architecture, and an architectural proposal is therefore also an organisational proposal. When two teams spend three weeks disagreeing about where a service boundary should sit, the technical arguments on both sides are often equally valid, because the real disagreement is about who will own the roadmap for the thing on either side of the line. The expert's tell is that the technical argument does not converge as evidence accumulates. The intervention is to settle ownership first and let the boundary follow.

"Engineering wants to refactor" is a claim about pain distribution

The naive reading is that engineers prefer clean code for aesthetic reasons. The accurate reading is almost always that a specific group of people is absorbing a specific recurring cost that is invisible to everyone else — the two production incidents a month, the four-hour deploy, the on-call that ruins a Thursday. The expert response is not to grant or refuse the refactor but to make the cost visible and let it compete: how many engineer-days a quarter does this consume, who bears them, and what does the curve look like in six months if we do nothing?

The technical veto runs on a credibility budget

An engineering leader who says "this is unsafe" three times a year and is right will be believed for a decade. One who says it monthly will be overridden within two quarters, including on the occasion when they are right and it matters. Experienced engineering leaders ration the hard "no" deliberately, and experienced product managers help them do it by distinguishing out loud between "this is more expensive than you think" and "this will lose data". The tell that the budget is exhausted: a product manager who has begun to route around an engineer rather than argue with them.

Silence in refinement is the strongest available signal

Retrospectives produce the feedback people are willing to say in a structured setting with a facilitator present. Refinement sessions produce something more reliable: whether engineers are curious. A team that asks no questions about a piece of work is not a team that understands it; it is a team that has stopped believing the answers will change anything. An expert product manager treats three consecutive silent refinements as a five-alarm signal, well before it shows up in velocity or attrition.

Escalation is a feature, and the order of escalation is diagnostic

Healthy relationships escalate — some disagreements genuinely require a more senior view, and pretending otherwise produces slow, resentful compromise. What matters is who escalates first and whether the other party learns about it from them or from their manager. The expert norm is simple and rarely written down: either party may escalate, and neither escalates without telling the other in the same hour. When escalation arrives as a surprise, the relationship has moved from disagreement to politics, and the recovery is measured in quarters.

The product manager's calendar is a production dependency

The decision-latency arithmetic above makes this concrete, but the nuance is subtler: what matters is not average response time but predictability. A product manager who answers within four hours reliably is more valuable than one who usually answers in twenty minutes and occasionally disappears for three days, because the first allows the team to plan around them and the second forces them to guess. The tell is engineers making product decisions in your absence and not mentioning it — which looks like autonomy and is actually the team routing around a flaky dependency.

Feedback on an implementation must separate "wrong" from "not what I pictured"

When a product manager sees a built feature and dislikes it, there are three distinct claims available: this does not solve the problem, this solves the problem in a way that will not scale, or this is not the shape I imagined. The first is squarely the product manager's to make. The second is a shared question. The third is, in most cases, not a legitimate objection at all, and delivering it as though it were the first is the single fastest way to lose an engineering team's trust. Experts announce which claim they are making before they make it.

Attrition is the real cost, and it lags by two quarters

A damaged relationship rarely shows up in this quarter's delivery numbers; teams under strain frequently deliver more in the short run, because heroics substitute for system health. It shows up two quarters later, when the two engineers who held the most context resign in the same month. The expert reads the leading indicators — silence in refinement, estimates that stop being decomposed, the disappearance of unsolicited proposals — because the lagging indicator arrives too late to act on.

7 Variation by product type and company stage

Some of the variation people assert here is real and some is folklore, and it is worth separating them. The real differences run along two axes: the reversibility of a decision, and the number of distinct customers whose interests are in tension.

In consumer software, reversibility is high and evidence is cheap, which shifts the exchange towards rapid, low-ceremony iteration and makes the specification school actively harmful. The characteristic pathology is the product manager as throughput manager: a stream of small tests, no accumulating argument, and engineers who slowly stop caring because nothing they build survives a quarter. In enterprise B2B, reversibility is moderate but evidence is expensive and biased — one customer's opinion arrives loudly and is mistaken for the market's — so the product manager's central obligation becomes filtering, and engineering's becomes making the product-versus-configuration distinction cheap in the architecture. That second point is where most enterprise software dies: the boundary between what is product and what is configured per customer is an architectural decision made early, on the basis of product judgement that was not available at the time.

In platform and infrastructure work, the relationship inverts: engineering is the customer, the product manager's value is in aggregation and sequencing rather than in user insight, and a product manager who cannot read a trace or reason about a latency budget will add no information to the exchange. In hardware-plus-software, as at Kshipra, the two halves of the product move at different clock speeds, and the relationship's main work is managing the coupling — deciding what must be in firmware, what can be pushed to the cloud, and therefore what may still be decided in June. In marketplaces, the distinguishing feature is that "the customer" is a contested term, and precision about which side is being served this quarter is not pedantry but the whole job.

Company stage changes the failure mode more than the principle, and here much of the received wisdom is overstated. The claim that small companies do not need the division of decision rights is false; they need it less formally, but a twenty-person company where the founder overrides the product manager weekly has exactly the same pathology as a two-thousand-person one, just faster. What genuinely changes is the mechanism of information flow: at twenty people it is osmotic and the risk is that reasoning is never written down, so it evaporates when the third engineer leaves; at two thousand it is documented and the risk is that nothing is read, so the exchange degrades into ticket-passing unless someone insists on direct contact with users and with each other.

8 Three worked examples, including one that failed

Amrai Fresh: the value of shipping the cheap version first

Rhea's disagreement with Kabir resolved itself once someone did the arithmetic in front of both of them. The full personalised model, requiring Kabir's nine-week rewrite, was expected to reach 58 per cent. Average recovered basket value per accepted substitution: ₹64.

Devika's case rested on a number Suresh did not initially have. Kshipra shipped about 42,000 GX-4 units a year. A field firmware update requiring a technician visit cost ₹2,900 per unit. In the previous hardware generation, three of the eleven utilities Kshipra served had eventually asked for a different sampling rate, affecting roughly 6,100 units, at a recovered cost of about ₹1.77 crore over the product's life — a cost absorbed quietly by the field-services budget and never attributed to the firmware decision that caused it.

Against that, six weeks of firmware and validation work at a loaded cost of around ₹22 lakh. Devika's argument was therefore not "customers want configurability" — a statement Suresh had heard and discounted for years — but "we have paid ₹1.77 crore twice now for not having it, and the insurance premium is ₹22 lakh." The expected-value case survives even at a much lower probability of recurrence. What made it work was that the cost sat in a different budget from the one Suresh was measured on, and nobody had previously done the arithmetic across the boundary.

Nishith Health Platforms: a relationship that failed, and what recovery cost

The instructive case is a failure. Nishith Health Platforms, a Hyderabad company selling operating-theatre scheduling software to hospital groups, committed in June to a multi-site rollout by 30 September. The product manager treated the date as fixed and the scope as fixed, and the engineering team — young, and unpractised at making the veto stick — absorbed the difference by taking shortcuts it disclosed in stand-ups but never priced: scheduling conflicts resolved in application code rather than the database, no migration path for the tenant model, and a test suite deliberately left thin.

The rollout happened on time. The consequences arrived from January. Squad velocity, measured in completed items per sprint, fell from 41 to 23 over two quarters as engineers spent increasing time on conflict-resolution defects. Two senior engineers, both of whom had raised the tenant-model problem in writing in July, resigned in the same fortnight in February; replacement cost, including recruitment fees and fourteen weeks of ramp at reduced output, came to roughly ₹24 lakh apiece in direct terms and considerably more in lost context. The tenant-model work that had been skipped in September took eleven weeks in March, because by then there was live data in four hospital groups to migrate.

The recovery is worth recording precisely, because it was not cultural. Nishith's new product manager and engineering manager established three mechanisms: a written debt register in which every shortcut was recorded with an estimated recurring cost and a review date; a standing 20 per cent allocation to that register, defended in planning; and a rule that no external commitment could be made without a named engineer having reviewed the decomposition. Velocity returned to 38 by the following October. The lesson practitioners draw from cases like this is usually "listen to your engineers", which is true and useless. The operative lesson is narrower: the shortcuts were disclosed but never priced, and disclosure without pricing is not information.
