10 Where thoughtful practitioners genuinely disagree

Four disagreements in this field are live, and a page that resolved them would be lying.

Should estimates exist at all? The forecasting school holds that a team's historical throughput, run through a Monte Carlo simulation, produces better delivery forecasts than item-by-item estimation, and does so at a fraction of the cost — the evidence being that throughput distributions are reasonably stable while individual estimates are not, and that estimation sessions consume meaningful engineering time to produce numbers nobody later checks. The estimation school responds that the act of estimating is where hidden complexity is discovered, that the number is a by-product of a conversation whose real value is shared understanding, and that a forecast from historical throughput is worthless for work unlike anything the team has done. Both positions rest on real evidence. What would have to be true for the forecasting school to be wrong: that teams doing genuinely novel work — Kshipra's firmware team, say — have throughput distributions too unstable to extrapolate. What would have to be true for the estimation school to be wrong: that the discovery of complexity happens equally well in a design discussion that produces no number.

Must a product manager be technical? One camp holds that without the ability to read the system, a product manager cannot evaluate a technical claim and is therefore reduced to trusting or overriding, neither of which is judgement. The steelman is strongest in platform and infrastructure contexts, where the customer is an engineer and a non-technical product manager genuinely adds no information. The other camp holds that technical depth without restraint reliably produces design-by-product-manager, that the scarce skill is holding a trade-off and not changing the answer, and that the most effective product managers in consumer businesses are frequently the least technical. Both camps can produce successful practitioners. The disagreement is probably a confusion of two variables — depth and restraint — that happen to be negatively correlated in practice.

Is the empowered-team model viable outside consumer software? Its advocates argue that regulated and hardware contexts differ only in the cost of a mistake, not in kind, and that safety-critical industries such as aviation have long combined strict specification with high team autonomy. Its sceptics argue that "give the team the problem, not the solution" is unworkable when the solution must be certified before it exists, and that the model is a luxury of businesses whose mistakes are cheap. Devika at Kshipra is living inside this disagreement, and her practical answer — empowered on everything before the freeze, specified on everything after — is a compromise neither camp fully endorses.

Does psychological safety cause performance, or follow it? The relational school's evidence is largely correlational: high-performing organisations exhibit generative information flow. The sceptical reading is that success produces safety rather than the reverse — teams that are winning find it easy to admit mistakes. The question matters practically, because it determines whether a leader facing a struggling team should invest in the relationship or in shipping something. Nobody has a clean answer, and the honest position is that the causation probably runs both ways with a lag.

11 What mastery actually looks like

Someone who has internalised this behaves differently in ways that are observable from across a room. They bring problems with the stakes attached and the acceptable failure already named, rather than solutions with dates attached. They ask what would narrow an estimate rather than arguing with it. They can state, without notes, what their team traded away in the last release and when the bill falls due. They defend unallocated capacity in planning meetings against their own short-term interest, because they understand the utilisation curve and have done the arithmetic on their own response time. They announce which kind of objection they are making before they make it. They know how much credibility their engineering counterpart has spent this quarter on hard refusals, and they help them spend it well. And when they disagree, they escalate openly and tell their counterpart in the same hour — because they understand that the asset being protected is not any one decision but the willingness of the other side to keep telling them things.

The person who has merely studied this can recite the division of value, usability and feasibility, runs impeccable ceremonies, and is nonetheless quietly routed around, because the team has learned that telling them the truth does not change what happens next.

12 What each protagonist decided

Rhea shipped the heuristic on 28 March, four days before her quarter closed, and used the seventy days of acceptance data it generated as the training set for the personalised model. She also conceded something she had resisted for two quarters: a standing 20 per cent unallocated band across the six squads, which she defended in April planning against a sales escalation. Her reasoning was that the platform read path was the binding constraint on three squads at once, and that no amount of arguing within the cart squad's decision rights could relieve it — the fix was an allocation decision, and it belonged above her.

Devika did not get the configurable sampling rate into GX-4. She got something more durable: Kshipra instituted a requirements-freeze review six weeks ahead of each firmware freeze, at which product and firmware jointly price every candidate against the field-service cost of not having it. The sampling rate went into GX-5 with three weeks to spare. Her reasoning was that her real failure had not been losing the argument in March; it was surfacing the requirement in March, when the decision structure required it in January.

Discussion questions.

1. Kabir's nine-week estimate was accurate and his recommendation was wrong. Under what conditions is a correct technical judgement still the wrong answer to a product question, and whose job is it to notice?

2. At Nishith, the shortcuts were disclosed in stand-ups and recorded in no artefact. If disclosure without pricing is not information, what exactly is the minimum viable pricing mechanism a ten-person team could sustain, and who owns it?

3. Devika concluded that her error was one of timing rather than argument. Is that self-assessment complete, or is it a comfortable way of avoiding the question of why firmware and product operate on separate planning calendars in the first place?

13 Going deeper

What a product manager does — the ownership boundaries assumed throughout this page are derived there; if the role definition is unclear, every decision-rights argument above becomes unresolvable.

How PMs alienate engineers — the same failure modes examined from the other side of the table, where they register as disrespect rather than as process error, which is why they are rarely reported upward.

Giving feedback on implementations — the moment this page deliberately compressed into a single nuance: separating "this does not solve the problem" from "this is not the shape I pictured" is where more trust is destroyed than in any estimate conversation.

The software development lifecycle — supplies the vocabulary for where in the cycle each piece of information must arrive, and explains why Devika's timing error was structural rather than personal.

Agile in practice — the tempo layer that sits on top of this relationship; useful precisely to the degree that you can already tell ceremony from substance, and dangerous before that.

Kanban and flow — the formal treatment of the utilisation curve and Little's Law sketched in section three, including work-in-progress limits as the practical instrument for buying responsiveness.

The execution rhythm — how the exchange is scheduled: which conversations happen daily, which weekly, which quarterly, and what breaks when a decision arrives on the wrong cadence.

Engineering estimates and T-shirt sizing — the distributional treatment of estimates, and the assumption audit that converts a wide range into a cheap experiment.

Backlog management and refinement — the operational surface on which most of this relationship is actually conducted, and the place where the silence diagnostic is run.
